hypothesis: If lateral-spined (S. mansoni) and terminal-spined (S. haematobium) eggs are mechanical variants produced by one species, then worms assigned to S. mansoni and to S. haematobium belong to one interbreeding lineage: their mitochondrial cox1 sequences should be no more divergent from each other than sequences within either nominal species, and should not form two reciprocally separated clusters.
pass_criterion: Pre-registered (claim supported). Using GenBank cox1 sequences (up to 40 per nominal species, chosen by a fixed random seed from all records >= 400 bp, hybrids excluded by title), pairwise uncorrected p-distances computed on pairwise alignments over >= 300 overlapping sites: the mean S. mansoni vs S. haematobium distance is <= 0.03, or the distributions overlap (minimum between-group distance smaller than the maximum within-group distance of either species, i.e. no barcode gap).
fail_criterion: Pre-registered (claim refuted). The minimum S. mansoni vs S. haematobium distance exceeds the maximum within-species distance of both S. mansoni and S. haematobium (complete barcode gap), the mean between-group distance is >= 0.10, and that mean is at least as large as the mean distance between each of two universally recognised distinct species pairs measured the same way (S. haematobium vs S. bovis; S. mansoni vs S. rodhaini). Any other combination is 'mixed'. If fewer than 10 usable sequences per focal species can be retrieved the verdict is 'inconclusive' (data-unavailable).
interpretation: Thompson's compound claim has two parts: (i) a mechanism (the lateral spine is moulded in a funnel-shaped part of the uterus), and (ii) the taxonomic conclusion he draws from it, that the two egg forms 'do not shew the existence of a separate species, S. mansoni'. Part (i) is anatomical and is not operationalizable with public data; part (ii) is tested here by genetic species delimitation, which did not exist in 1917 (modern reinterpretation: 'separate species' is read as a separately evolving, reproductively isolated lineage, detectable as a deep, reciprocally separated mitochondrial divergence comparable to that between other accepted Schistosoma species). GenBank species labels for sequenced adult worms rest on life-cycle, host and multilocus data, not only on egg-spine position, which limits the circularity noted by the assessors.
